title: Quibi: How to Lose $1.75 Billion in Six Months
creator: Rosa Delgado
description:
The short, expensive life of Quibi, the streaming app built for your phone that nobody watched on their phone.

Sources: launch coverage, the shutdown letter, interviews with former staff. Full list in the pinned comment.

0:00 The pitch
1:05 Turnstyle
2:00 Launch week
3:10 Why it died
4:15 What it left behind

sentences.t: In April of twenty twenty, a streaming service launched with one point seven five billion dollars in the bank.
It had shows from Steven Spielberg, it had Reese Witherspoon, it had a Super Bowl ad.
And six months later it was gone, sold for parts, like it never existed.
That service was Quibi, and the story of how it died is honestly one of the strangest in tech.
Quibi was the idea of Jeffrey Katzenberg, the guy who helped bring us The Lion King and Shrek.
His pitch was simple, people watch video on their phones in little gaps, on the bus, in a queue.
So why not make Hollywood quality shows, chopped into chapters of ten minutes or less, made only for phones?
Quick bites, that's literally where the name comes from, Quibi, quick bites.
He brought in Meg Whitman, the former CEO of eBay and HP, to run it.
And investors just poured money in, Disney, NBC, Alibaba, basically every studio you can name.
Now, the product itself had one genuinely clever idea, and they were very proud of it.
They called it Turnstyle, and it meant every Quibi show was shot twice, once for portrait and once for landscape.
You turned your phone sideways and the Quibi app cut seamlessly to the other version without pausing.
Quibi charged four ninety nine a month with ads, or seven ninety nine without, after a ninety day free trial.
At launch Quibi had a library of fifty shows and promised to add more than a hundred and seventy-five in the first year.
On paper, Quibi looked like the future of mobile video, and a lot of very smart people believed it.
And then it launched, the first week of April twenty twenty.
You might remember what else was happening that week.
Everyone was stuck at home, nobody was on a bus, nobody was standing in a queue.
The entire premise, watching in the little gaps of your day, disappeared overnight.
People were at home with big TVs, and at launch you couldn't even cast the app to a TV.
Then there were the screenshots, or rather, there weren't any.
The app blocked screenshots to protect the content, which sounds sensible until you realize that's how things go viral.
Nobody could clip a funny moment and post it, so nobody outside the app ever saw anything from it.
The one time it really trended was a horror short about a woman with a golden arm, and even that was mostly people making fun of it.
By the summer, reports said fewer than ten percent of free trial users were sticking around.
Katzenberg blamed the pandemic, publicly, in an interview, for basically everything.
And in October, just six months after launch, they announced they were shutting it all down.
They handed most of the money that was left back to investors, which almost never happens.
The shows themselves were sold to Roku for reportedly less than a hundred million dollars.
Some of them are still on there, if you go looking, and a few are actually pretty good.
So what's the lesson?
I think it's that a big budget can buy you famous names, but it can't buy you a habit people already have.
Everyone was already watching short videos on their phones, they were just watching them for free, made by people like me.
Anyway, let me know which dead startup you want me to cover next, I have a list and it's very long.
